newsitem.title: GERMANY: German economy to grow steadily in 97,98 - OECD.
newsitem.headline: German economy to grow steadily in 97,98 - OECD.

text.p: The German economy is likely to expand steadily in 1997 and 1998, with inflation holding at very low levels, but the continued growth will do little to help a depressed labour market, the OECD said on Thursday.

In a semi-annual report, the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development said the German economy would grow by 2.2 percent in 1997 and 2.6 percent in 1998 after just 1.1 percent in 1996--lower than many expect for this year.
The economy grew by 1.9 percent in 1995.
Inflation would hold near current levels, showing an average of 1.3 percent for 1996 and 1998 and dipping slightly to 1.2 percent in between, the forecasting group said.

Turning to fiscal performance, the OECD said it appeared that Germany could succeed in cutting its public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 to meet the entry grade for European Economic and Monetary Union.
But it warned that, to achieve this, all planned spending cuts had to be implemented strictly.
"It needs to be stressed that estimates of savings for entitlement programmes and health spending have often proved to be optimistic in the past," the OECD said.
"With little margin for safety, there is thus a risk that the 1997 budget target might not be achieved," it added.
Its actual forecast showed the general government deficit at 3.4 percent of GDP in 1997 and 2.6 percent in 1998.

Although it saw a chance of a further small easing in Bundesbank policy this year, the OECD said current conditions created a good basis for growth and that interest rates were thus likely to turn higher in the forecast period.

"A further short-term easing of monetary policy would be possible if the growth of the monetary stock and other forward-looking indicators becoming available in the coming quarters pointed to continued weakness and subdued inflation pressure for the period ahead," it said.
"Further into the projection period, hewever, short-term rates are likely to increase somewhat if the economy follows the projected course of recovery," the report added.

Positive impulses for growth also came from wage policies and the fiscal side. More moderate wage deals, combined with increased labour market flexibility, would help to improve profitability which in turn would boost domestic investment.
This would lend strength to the export-driven recovery.

"Nevertheless, whether the moderate wage round and the structural measures adopted by the government signal a fundamental change in labour market behaviour is at this stage unclear," the OECD said, adding that wage rises might therefore recover before the unemployment rate fell notably.
The unemployment rate was forecast to peak at 10.4 percent in 1997 before easing back only slightly to 10.1 in 1998.
The OECD gave the following forecasts for Germany (percentage change from previous year):
GDP at market prices 1.9 1.1 2.2 2.6
GDP deflator 2.2 1.3 1.2 1.3
Public sector balance (vs GDP) -3.5 -4.1 -3.4 -2.6
Unemployment rate 9.4 10.3 10.4 10.1
Compensation of employees 3.1 1.5 2.6 3.3
Short-term interest rate 4.5 3.3 3.1 3.7
Long-term interest rate 6.9 6.3 6.1 6.3
--Janet Northcote, Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525
